Please use the culture aware methods for producing these strings. If these  _aren't_ raising errors right now, they will when we upgrade the .net framework version. At the top of this file, you can add

``` csharp
using static QuantConnect.StringExtensions;
```
and then where ever you use string interpolation ( `$"{var}" syntax ) you can do the following:

``` csharp
$"{date:yyyMMdd}.zip#{index}"
```

If you don't like static usings (hey, what did they ever do to you!) you can use extension methods:

``` csharp
$"{date.ToStringInvariant(DateFormat.EightCharacter)}.zip#{index}"
```

I think the `Invariant(...)` is much sexier since it accepts as an argument the _interpolated_ string -- which is cool -- I didn't realize interpolated strings are *their own type* in C#.

The not empty predicate is there to attempt a recovery of the ticker in question if the exchange tag was for some reason omitted. 

`// Example: SPOT (Spotify) on 2018-10-01 has a missing exchange even though it has already IPO'd`

It's a little ugly, so I'll clarify what the purpose of the `string.IsNullOrEmpty` by creating a new parameter for this called `attemptRecovery` 👍

not applicable here, but an interesting and potentially headache-inducing side effect of using `FileInfo` is that they only load their data once -- the first time you access anything derived from the file's headers/options. You can update an instance of `FileInfo` manually by calling the `Refresh()` function. Here's an [SO thread](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/issues/42447) discussing it along with the [method documentation](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.io.filesysteminfo.refresh?view=netframework-4.8). You'll note this is pointing at `FileSystemInfo` -- which is the base class of `FileInfo` and he's the one that defines the `Refresh` function.

EDIT: You're totally all over this -- didn't see a usage of `FileSystemInfo.Refresh()` until hitting enter on this one. Leaving here for posterity.

seeing the `ToString()`'s everywhere is kind of unexpected. Per the [documentation](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_ToString.htm), the `ToString()` method on `JToken` and it's descendants is to:
> Returns the indented JSON for this token.

Whereas the `Value<T>(propertyName)` function ([docs](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_Value__1.htm)):
> Gets the `JToken` with the specified key converted to the specified type.
Why resolve this using the composer? Is that necessary?
Yes - this is for our backend operations and the need for flexibility there
If these were converted into objects above as suggested -- much of this code simplifies.

interesting -- I've never had good luck w/ `ToString()` on `JToken` derived types -- I've always had to use `Value<string>(propertyName)` -- oh yea -- probably because I would use it as:

``` csharp
JArray.Parse(item.Value<string>("bz:ticker"))
```

which I think is the way the library's documentation recommends you do it. By using the `Value<T>` accessors you get to lean on the framework to validate your assumptions regarding the type of the value. Probably not making a difference here, but can be useful information.

This `foreach` loop could be collapsed into the follow without losing readability (IMO):

``` csharp
tickers = JArray.Parse(item.Value<string>("bz:ticker")).ToList();
```

or using `AddRange` to save the list instance:

``` csharp
tickers.AddRange(JArray.Parse(item.Value<string>("bz:ticker")))
```

_also_ -- why not convert these into objects right away? You define all the required `[JsonProperty]` attributes -- you can do something like... `token.ToObject<BenzingaNews>()` ([docs](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_ToObject__1.htm))

what a strange json response style... I don't think I've ever seen `@` prefixes -- Do you know the story behind their prefixing pattern? I also noticed the `#` -- maybe it's a form of hungarian notation denoting the type in some way?

It's all about how Json.NET deals with serializing XML to JSON. It adds a `#` prefix to the inner element. An example is `1234` would show up as `#a` for `1234` and `@href` for `example`. I decided to go this way instead of using an auto-generated class from `xsd.exe` since I think it's a cleaner solution and bloats the codebase less (and makes it more understandable/maintainable too in my opinion)

totally style and feel free to ignore this, but my preference would be to use `OS.IsWindows` directly

Just a note for you 😄 : I avoided using `OS.IsWindows` since there is close to absolutely no possibility that we will have the OS switch on us while the program is running. In addition to that, since the property would perform a [few allocations per call](https://referencesource.microsoft.com/#mscorlib/system/environment.cs,7d2f1469d916fc63) (albeit probably in a low heap generation), it wouldn't matter. But what I'm concerned about is possible syscalls being made trying to identify the platform causing the processing to slow down since we're leaving userspace, especially in a hotter path.

Agreed with you that OS.IsWindows is much cleaner, but those were the design considerations I made when I chose to cache the `OS.IsWindows` call.

not a nit -- **why** are we using a `HashSet<T>` here at all? hash sets, or really sets in general, are great for two reasons, one is guaranteeing uniqueness and for `O(1)`  `Contains`/`Exists` calls. Do we expect the file at `referenceFilePath` to contain duplicates?

I suppose even if we _don't_ expect dupes, I'm sure it's nice being able to guarantee that no dupes will be written. it's nice to define _invariants_ like that -- helps you reason about code and more importantly, and downstream applications that might pick up this application's output -- such as algorithms 😄
